title: Red Flags When Hiring a Commercial Cleaning Company (And How to Spot Them Early)
excerpt: Most Newcastle businesses find out they've hired the wrong cleaning company 6 to 12 weeks after signing. These are the warning signs to look for before you commit — from vague quotes to no-show audits.
content:
## The mistake most businesses make

They find a cleaning company that seems fine on paper, sign the contract, and then spend the next several months managing the problem they just created. Calling the cleaner. Following up. Finding things that weren't done. Repeating instructions. Eventually the relationship sours, they start looking for a replacement, and the cycle begins again.

This is avoidable. The warning signs are there before you sign. You just have to know what to look for.

## Red flag 1: They won't visit the site before quoting

A commercial cleaner who quotes you over the phone, from a floor plan, or without seeing your space is not a cleaner who understands your space. They don't know how many bathrooms you have, what your floor surfaces are like, whether there are access restrictions, or how much foot traffic the entry areas handle.

That means their quote is based on assumptions. When the reality of your space doesn't match those assumptions, either your price goes up, or your service goes down. Neither is acceptable.

A professional cleaner will always want to see the space before they quote. If they don't, that's the first signal.

## Red flag 2: The scope of works is vague

If the proposal uses phrases like "general cleaning of all areas", "professional cleaning services", or "maintaining a high standard of cleanliness", you don't have a scope of works. You have a marketing document.

A real scope of works is specific. It names rooms, it names tasks, it names frequencies, it names what is and isn't included. It tells you who supplies toilet paper. It tells you whether internal glass is cleaned on every visit or monthly.

No cleaner should be offended by you asking for specifics. If the resistance starts before you've even signed, it's going to be worse after.

## Red flag 3: The price is significantly below market

In Newcastle in 2026, a commercial cleaner with proper insurance, direct employees, quality management, and a functioning business costs money. If someone is quoting $25 or $30 an hour where the market is clearly $45–$60 for equivalent service, that price is not the result of efficiency. It's the result of cutting something.

Usually it's staffing. Cheap cleaners have high turnover because they pay poorly. High turnover means your site is always being cleaned by someone who doesn't know it. The low price is exactly what it costs — and you'll pay for it in staff complaints, missed areas, and the eventual discovery that the bathroom wasn't cleaned last Tuesday.

## Red flag 4: No references from similar sites

A legitimate cleaning company with a track record can give you references. Not just testimonials on their website — actual contacts at businesses comparable to yours, who you can call and ask specific questions.

Ask for two or three. The most useful question to ask a reference is not "were you happy?" It's: "What happens when something goes wrong?" The answer to that question is the real measure of a cleaning company.

If they can't provide references or the references are all from three years ago, they probably don't have a long track record of consistent service.

## Red flag 5: Vague answers about insurance

Ask for a certificate of currency before you sign. It should show:

- Public liability of at least $10 million
- Workers compensation insurance for their employees
- An active, current policy

"Yes, we're fully insured" is not a certificate. If they can't produce one within 24 hours, they either don't have it, it's lapsed, or the coverage is inadequate. None of those options are your problem to inherit.

## Red flag 6: They can't tell you who's cleaning your space

If you ask "who will actually clean our office?" and the answer is "we have a team of cleaners" without naming a specific person or team assigned to your site, your space is going to be cleaned by whoever is available. That means rotating contractors, first-day-on-the-job nervousness, and no one who actually knows the layout.

Consistent service comes from consistent people. A company that can't tell you who is on your site is a company that doesn't manage its people well enough to assign them properly.

## Red flag 7: No quality audit process

A cleaning company that only responds to complaints is running a reactive service. They're not managing your standards — they're reacting when the standards slip enough that you notice and call them.

A proactive cleaner runs regular site audits. They inspect your space, identify problems before you do, and fix them. You get a report. If they can't describe this process to you before you've signed, they almost certainly don't have one.

## Red flag 8: Contract lock-in without a trial period

Cleaning contracts exist to protect both parties. But a contract that locks you in for 12 months with no trial or exit clause, before you've had a chance to see whether the service actually works, is a contract written to benefit the cleaner.

A reasonable contract should have a short initial period — 30 to 60 days — where either party can exit with reasonable notice and no penalty. That gives you time to see if the service actually delivers. If they won't agree to this, think carefully about why.

## The one question that catches them all

If you want a single question that surfaces most of these issues before you've signed: ask them to describe their quality management process. Not whether they're good at cleaning — how they make sure the standard is maintained across every visit, every week, for the life of the contract.

A vague answer means a vague service. A specific, practiced answer means a company that actually runs itself professionally.
